lab.title: Histology
lab.blurb: the four tissue types under the microscope

facts.location: Alveoli of the lungs; lining of blood vessels (endothelium); serous membranes
facts.definition: A single layer of flat, scale-like cells with flattened nuclei; allows rapid diffusion and filtration.

facts.location: Kidney tubules; thyroid follicles; liver
facts.definition: A single layer of cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei; absorption and secretion.

facts.location: Lining of the stomach, intestines, gallbladder, uterus and uterine tubes
facts.definition: A single layer of tall cells with oval nuclei near the base; often has goblet cells and microvilli.

facts.location: Trachea and upper respiratory tract
facts.definition: A single layer whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks layered; every cell touches the basement membrane. Usually ciliated with goblet cells.

facts.location: Epidermis, especially palms and soles
facts.definition: Many layers; surface cells are dead, flat, and packed with keratin, so no nuclei are visible at the surface.

facts.location: Mouth, esophagus, vagina
facts.definition: Many layers; surface cells are flat but alive and still have nuclei. Moist surfaces subject to abrasion.

facts.location: Ducts of sweat and salivary glands
facts.definition: Two or more layers of cube-shaped cells lining a duct.

facts.location: Urinary bladder, ureters, urinary tract
facts.definition: Multilayered with rounded, dome-shaped surface cells that flatten when the organ stretches.

facts.location: Beneath nearly every epithelium; papillary layer of the dermis; around blood vessels
facts.definition: Loose, random web of thin collagen and elastic fibers with scattered fibroblasts and lots of ground substance.

facts.location: Lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow
facts.definition: A mesh of thin, branching fibers that supports blood-forming and lymphatic organs.

facts.location: Tendons and ligaments
facts.definition: Parallel, tightly packed collagen bundles with rows of flattened fibroblast nuclei between them.

facts.location: Dermis of the skin; capsules around organs
facts.definition: Thick collagen bundles running in many directions, resisting stress from any angle.

facts.location: Subcutaneous fat; around organs such as the kidneys and heart
facts.definition: Large, empty-looking adipocytes with the nucleus pushed to one edge (signet-ring appearance).

facts.location: Trachea, costal cartilages, nose, articular surfaces of bones
facts.definition: Glassy, smooth matrix with chondrocytes sitting in lacunae, often in pairs; no visible fibers.

facts.location: External ear, epiglottis
facts.definition: Chondrocytes in lacunae surrounded by a dense web of dark-staining, stretchy fibers.

facts.location: Intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci of the knee
facts.definition: Chondrocytes lined up in rows between thick, visible bundles of collagen.

facts.location: The hard outer shell of the skeleton and the shafts of the long limb elements
facts.definition: Hard, calcified matrix arranged in osteons: concentric lamellae around a central canal with osteocytes in lacunae.

facts.location: Ends of long bones; interior of flat bones
facts.definition: A lattice of thin plates (trabeculae) with marrow spaces between them; no osteons.

facts.location: Inside arteries, veins, and capillaries
facts.definition: Fluid connective tissue: liquid plasma matrix with erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. Classified as connective because it develops from mesenchyme and has cells scattered in an extracellular matrix.

facts.location: Muscles attached to bones: limbs, head and neck, trunk
facts.definition: Long, unbranched, striated fibers with many nuclei pushed to the edge of each fiber. Voluntary.

facts.location: Heart only
facts.definition: Short, branched, striated cells with a single central nucleus, joined end to end by intercalated discs. Involuntary.

facts.location: Walls of hollow organs: stomach, intestines, bladder, blood vessels
facts.definition: Short spindle-shaped cells with one central cigar-shaped nucleus and no striations. Involuntary.

facts.location: Brain, spinal cord, nerves
facts.definition: Large star-shaped neurons with a prominent nucleus and nucleolus and many processes, surrounded by small glial cells.
A mucus-secreting cell wedged among columnar cells; looks like a pale wine glass.
Hair-like projections on the free surface that sweep mucus along.
A dark transverse line where two cardiac muscle cells join; passes electrical signals between cells.
Alternating light and dark bands along a muscle fiber.
A small cavity in cartilage or bone matrix that houses a cell.
A mature cartilage cell sitting in a lacuna.
A mature bone cell trapped in a lacuna between lamellae.
The basic unit of compact bone: concentric lamellae around a central canal.
The channel at the center of an osteon carrying blood vessels and nerves.
Concentric rings of calcified matrix around a central canal.
A biconcave disc with no nucleus that carries oxygen.
A nucleated blood cell of the immune system; a neutrophil has a multilobed nucleus.
Small cell fragments that clump together to begin clotting.
One large lipid droplet with the nucleus flattened against the cell membrane (signet-ring look).
The spindle-shaped cell that makes the fibers and ground substance of connective tissue.
Thick, tough, pink-staining protein fibers that resist tension.
The signal-conducting cell of nervous tissue: cell body, dendrites, and one axon.
Small supporting cells that protect and nourish neurons but do not conduct long-distance signals.
The thin layer anchoring an epithelium to the connective tissue beneath it.

questions.prompt: Which criterion distinguishes simple epithelium from stratified epithelium?
options: The presence or absence of a basement membrane
The type of fiber in the matrix

questions.prompt: Which connective tissue subtype is found in tendons and ligaments, and is characterized by parallel collagen fibers?
A tissue sample shows a single layer of cells, but the nuclei appear at different levels, giving a false impression of multiple layers. What is the tissue type?
What muscle tissue type is involuntary, has branched striated cells with a single central nucleus, and uses intercalated discs to pass electrical signals between cells?
Which two cell types make up nervous tissue, and what distinguishes their roles?
options: Cardiomyocytes and neurons; both transmit electrical signals equally
Neurons and erythrocytes; neurons signal, erythrocytes carry oxygen
Neurons and glial cells; neurons transmit signals, glial cells support and protect but don't transmit long-distance signals
Adipocytes and osteocytes; adipocytes store energy, osteocytes provide structure

questions.prompt: Why is pseudostratified columnar epithelium classified as simple rather than stratified, despite its appearance?
questions.modelAnswer: Every cell touches the basement membrane, so there is only one true layer. The nuclei sit at different heights because the cells are different heights, which fakes the look of layers.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between keratinized and nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and how does it relate to where each is found?
questions.modelAnswer: Keratinized: the surface layers are dead, flattened, and filled with keratin with no nuclei; found on dry, abraded surfaces such as the epidermis (palms, soles). Nonkeratinized: surface cells are alive and still have nuclei; found on moist internal surfaces such as the mouth, esophagus, and vagina.

questions.prompt: Name one structural feature that distinguishes dense regular connective tissue from dense irregular connective tissue.
questions.modelAnswer: In dense regular tissue the collagen bundles run parallel in one direction (tendons pull one way); in dense irregular tissue the bundles run in many directions (dermis resists stress from any angle).

questions.prompt: What structure would you look for to confirm you are viewing cardiac muscle rather than skeletal muscle?
questions.modelAnswer: Intercalated discs: dark transverse lines between cells. Also branching fibers and a single central nucleus, versus skeletal muscle's long unbranched fibers with many peripheral nuclei.

questions.prompt: Cheek cells swabbed onto a slide look like simple squamous epithelium, yet the cheek lining is stratified squamous (nonkeratinized). Why might the swabbed cells appear as a single scattered layer?
questions.modelAnswer: The swab only scrapes off the loose surface cells, which spread out individually on the slide. The deeper layers stay attached in the cheek, so the slide shows single flat cells rather than the intact multilayered tissue.

questions.prompt: Explain why blood is classified as a connective tissue even though it doesn't look like the other connective tissues.
questions.modelAnswer: Like all connective tissues it consists of cells scattered in an abundant extracellular matrix (plasma) and develops from embryonic mesenchyme. Its matrix is liquid and its fibers (fibrin) only appear during clotting, which is why it looks different.

questions.prompt: How do you tell hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and fibrocartilage apart on a slide?
questions.modelAnswer: Hyaline: smooth glassy matrix with no visible fibers, chondrocytes in lacunae. Elastic: dark web of elastic fibers around the lacunae. Fibrocartilage: thick visible collagen bundles with chondrocytes lined up in rows between them.

questions.prompt: What do muscle tissue and nervous tissue have in common?
questions.modelAnswer: Both are excitable: they can sense and react to electrochemical stimuli by changing their membrane potential.
